front: How does small cell lung cancer behave differently from non-small cell lung cancer?
back: It is a fast-growing neuroendocrine tumor that spreads early (especially to the brain), so it is treated mainly with chemo ± radiation rather than surgery.
extra: About 15% of lung cancers, almost always in smokers. Staged as limited vs extensive instead of by TNM groupings.

front: What is the most common lung cancer histology, and where in the lung does it usually arise?
back: Adenocarcinoma, usually peripheral
extra: It is also the most common type in never-smokers and carries most of the targetable driver mutations.

front: Which two lung cancer histologies classically arise centrally?
back: Squamous cell and small cell
extra: Both S's sit in the Center. Both are strongly tied to smoking.

front: What is the leading cause of lung cancer in never-smokers?
back: Radon
extra: A radioactive gas from soil that collects in basements. It is the #2 cause overall, after smoking.

front: A smoker with a central lung mass has hyponatremia from SIADH. Which histology is most likely?
back: Small cell lung cancer
extra: Small cell also causes ectopic ACTH and Lambert-Eaton. Squamous cell is the classic cause of hypercalcemia (PTHrP).

front: Why is every nonsquamous NSCLC tested for driver mutations and PD-L1?
back: The results change systemic therapy: a driver mutation (e.g., EGFR, ALK) means a targeted pill instead of immunotherapy, and PD-L1 guides how much immunotherapy is used.
extra: This now matters for early-stage and stage III disease too, not just metastatic disease.

front: Which driver mutation is classic in a young woman who never smoked and has lung adenocarcinoma?
back: EGFR
extra: Targeted with osimertinib. ALK is the other classic never-smoker driver.

front: Who qualifies for lung cancer screening (USPSTF), and with what test?
back: Annual low-dose CT for ages 50-80 with ≥20 pack-years who currently smoke or quit within the last 15 years
extra: NLST showed a 20% relative reduction in lung cancer deaths. Screening finds the small peripheral tumors that often become SBRT patients.

front: Which lung tumors move the most with breathing, and why does that matter for radiation?
back: Lower lobe tumors (often 1-2 cm or more). Their motion has to be measured (4D-CT) and covered or controlled during planning.
extra: Large motion is managed with abdominal compression, gating, or breath hold rather than a bigger margin.

front: What makes a lung tumor "central" for SBRT?
back: Within 2 cm of the proximal bronchial tree (trachea, carina, main and lobar bronchi) or touching the mediastinal or pericardial pleura
extra: The 2 cm "no-fly zone." Central tumors cannot safely get 3-fraction SBRT.

front: What makes a lung tumor "ultracentral"?
back: The tumor (or its PTV) touches or overlaps the proximal bronchial tree, trachea, or esophagus.
extra: The highest-risk location for SBRT: treated with 8 or more fractions or conventional fractionation.

front: What causes the classic symptoms of a superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor?
back: Invasion of the lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) and stellate ganglion: shoulder/arm pain, hand weakness, and Horner syndrome
extra: Often missed as "apical pleural thickening." MRI best shows plexus, vessel, and vertebral invasion.

front: What N stage is a subcarinal (station 7) node, regardless of tumor side?
back: N2
extra: Station 7 drains both lungs, so it always counts as ipsilateral. It is the most commonly involved mediastinal station.

front: Is a supraclavicular node in lung cancer N3 or M1?
back: N3 (either side). It is regional, so the patient can still be treated for cure.
extra: Contralateral mediastinal or hilar nodes are the other way to be N3.

front: What does FDG PET/CT add to lung cancer staging?
back: It stages the nodes and distant disease (N and M) for every patient treated with curative intent.
extra: It upstages a meaningful share of patients compared with CT alone. For radiation, it also separates hot tumor from cooler atelectasis when drawing the GTV.

front: Why does a PET-positive mediastinal node usually need tissue confirmation before it changes the plan?
back: Inflammation and infection (TB, fungal disease, sarcoidosis, pneumonia) also light up on PET, so hot is not always cancer.
extra: PET finds the nodes; EBUS proves them.

front: Which lung cancer patients need a brain MRI as part of staging?
back: NSCLC stage II and above (consider for IB) and every patient with small cell
extra: PET cannot screen the brain because normal brain is always FDG-avid.

front: What CT features make a lung nodule suspicious for cancer (margin, texture, and behavior over time)?
back: Spiculated margin, part-solid texture, and growth
extra: Also upper lobe and larger size (>3 cm = a mass). Reassuring: smooth margin, benign calcification, fat, 2-year stability.

front: In a part-solid adenocarcinoma, which part is measured for the T stage?
back: Only the solid (invasive) component
extra: The ground-glass part is usually non-invasive lepidic growth.

front: On a lung radiation plan, what is the ITV, and what scan is used to build it?
back: The internal target volume: the GTV's position across the whole breathing cycle, built from a 4D-CT simulation
extra: GTV → ITV → (CTV for stage III) → PTV. Daily cone-beam CT lines the tumor up before each SBRT fraction.

front: A mass-like opacity appears at the SBRT site 6 months after treatment. What is it most likely, and what would suggest recurrence instead?
back: Expected radiation fibrosis. Recurrence is suggested by enlargement after 12 months, a bulging margin, or loss of air bronchograms.
extra: Fibrosis conforms to the high-dose region and stabilizes. Suspicious changes get PET/CT and biopsy; don't call recurrence too early.

front: When choosing which site to biopsy in suspected lung cancer, what is the guiding principle?
back: Biopsy the site that would give the highest stage, so one procedure diagnoses and stages at the same time.
extra: Examples: EBUS of a suspicious mediastinal node, thoracentesis of an effusion, or biopsy of a single suspected metastasis.

front: What is the first-line procedure for sampling mediastinal lymph nodes in lung cancer?
back: EBUS-guided needle aspiration (endobronchial ultrasound)
extra: It reaches stations 2, 4, 7, 10, and 11. Mediastinoscopy is added if EBUS is negative but suspicion remains; stations 5 and 6 need a Chamberlain procedure or VATS.

front: Which lung cancer patients can skip invasive mediastinal staging?
back: Those with a small (≤3 cm) peripheral tumor and a clean PET/CT mediastinum
extra: Central tumors, tumors >3 cm, and any suspicious hilar or mediastinal node get EBUS. This matters before SBRT, which treats the primary only.

front: In early-stage NSCLC, what usually decides surgery vs SBRT?
back: The patient's fitness for surgery (mainly lung function on PFTs: FEV1 and DLCO), not the tumor
extra: Predicted postoperative FEV1 and DLCO >60% = low surgical risk; very poor function favors SBRT.

front: What are the size cutoffs for T1 through T4 in lung cancer?
extra: Invasion beats size: a small tumor that invades a T3 or T4 structure takes that higher T. Subcategories (T1a-c, T2a-b) live in the AJCC tables.

front: What is the general difference between T3 and T4 invasion in lung cancer?
back: T3 = the lung's outer boundaries (chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium). T4 = the mediastinum and its contents (heart, great vessels, trachea/carina, esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve), plus vertebral body or diaphragm.
extra: Clinical clue: an elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic) is T3; new hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal nerve in the AP window) is T4.

front: How is a separate tumor nodule staged if it is in the same lobe, a different lobe of the same lung, or the other lung?
back: Same lobe = T3. Different ipsilateral lobe = T4. Contralateral lung = M1a.
extra: The farther the nodule, the higher the stage.

front: What separates N1, N2, and N3 in lung cancer?
back: N1 = ipsilateral hilar/intrapulmonary nodes (stations 10-14). N2 = ipsilateral mediastinal nodes (stations 2-9). N3 = contralateral mediastinal/hilar or any supraclavicular nodes.
extra: Double digits = hilum, single digits = mediastinum. AJCC 9th edition splits N2 into one station (N2a) vs several (N2b).

front: What does a malignant pleural effusion do to the stage of a lung cancer?
back: It is M1a: stage IV disease
extra: M1a = spread within the chest (effusion, pleural nodules, contralateral lung). M1b = a single extrathoracic met; M1c = multiple.

front: What separates limited-stage from extensive-stage small cell lung cancer?
back: Limited stage is confined to one hemithorax and its regional nodes and can be covered by one tolerable radiation field. Anything beyond that is extensive.
extra: Limited stage is treated for cure with concurrent chemoradiation. About 2/3 of patients present with extensive stage.

front: What is the standard treatment for node-negative early-stage NSCLC in a patient fit for surgery?
back: Lobectomy with lymph node dissection or sampling
extra: Segmentectomy is an option for peripheral tumors ≤2 cm. No routine radiation after a complete resection.

front: What is the standard treatment for node-negative early-stage NSCLC in a patient who cannot have surgery?
back: SBRT alone (no chemotherapy)
extra: Local control is around 90-95% (RTOG 0236). The main side effect is usually mild pneumonitis.

front: Why isn't SBRT used for node-positive NSCLC?
back: SBRT treats only the primary tumor. Once nodes are involved they must be in the field, so an inoperable patient gets concurrent chemoradiation instead.
extra: This is why the nodes are confirmed negative (PET ± EBUS) before SBRT.

front: How does tumor location change SBRT fractionation for early-stage lung cancer?
back: The closer to the middle of the chest, the more fractions: peripheral about 3 (e.g., 54 Gy/3), central 5 (e.g., 50 Gy/5, never 3), ultracentral 8 or more
extra: Tumors abutting the chest wall often get 4-5 fractions to limit rib fracture and chest wall pain.

front: What is the feared toxicity when treating an ultracentral lung tumor with SBRT?
back: Fatal hemoptysis (and fistula) from high dose to the main airways or esophagus
extra: In HILUS, about 15% of patients died of treatment, mostly from bleeding. Here toxicity, not tumor control, drives the plan.

front: What biologic dose target do lung SBRT regimens aim for, and why?
back: A BED10 of at least 100 Gy, because local control drops below that
extra: 54 Gy in 3 fractions and 50 Gy in 5 fractions both clear this bar.

front: What is the standard treatment sequence for a resectable superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor?
back: Neoadjuvant concurrent chemoradiation (~45-50 Gy), then surgery, then more systemic therapy
extra: SWOG 9416 / INT 0160: complete resection in over 90%. Unresectable → definitive chemoRT; watch the brachial plexus dose.

front: What is the standard treatment for unresectable stage III NSCLC?
back: Concurrent chemoradiation to 60 Gy in 30 fractions, then durvalumab for 1 year (osimertinib instead if EGFR-mutant)
extra: PACIFIC (durvalumab) and LAURA (osimertinib) both improved outcomes after chemoRT.

front: Why isn't stage III NSCLC treated to doses higher than 60 Gy?
back: RTOG 0617: 74 Gy gave worse overall survival than 60 Gy.
extra: Heart dose predicted death, which is why cardiac sparing matters in lung plans.

front: In definitive chemoradiation for stage III NSCLC, which lymph nodes are included in the target?
back: Only involved nodes (PET-positive or biopsy-proven) with the primary; no elective nodal irradiation
extra: This keeps lung, esophagus, and heart doses down.

front: What is the modern approach for resectable stage III NSCLC (e.g., single-station, non-bulky N2)?
back: Neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, then surgery
extra: CheckMate 816 raised the complete response rate from 2% to 24%. Radiation is reserved for a positive margin.

front: When is postoperative radiation (PORT) indicated after NSCLC resection?
back: For a positive margin, not routinely for resected N2 disease with clear margins
extra: LungART: PORT after complete resection of N2 disease did not improve disease-free survival and added heart and lung toxicity.

front: When does radiation pneumonitis typically appear, and which dose metrics predict it?
back: About 1-6 months after RT. Predicted by lung V20 (keep <30-35%) and mean lung dose (keep <20 Gy).
extra: Classic symptoms are cough, dyspnea, and low-grade fever; it is treated with steroids.

front: Which acute toxicity is most expected during conventional thoracic chemoradiation, and when does it start?
back: Esophagitis (painful swallowing), starting around weeks 2-3
extra: Mean esophagus dose is kept under about 34 Gy.

front: What is the role of radiation in oligometastatic NSCLC?
back: SBRT to every site of disease (local consolidative therapy) alongside systemic therapy
extra: Usually ≤3-5 stable or responding metastases. Gomez and SABR-COMET showed better survival. A single brain met gets SRS.

front: A patient with metastatic lung cancer has worsening hemoptysis. What kind of radiation course fits?
back: A short palliative course chosen by prognosis and goals (e.g., 30 Gy/10, 20 Gy/5, or 10 Gy/1), not 6 weeks of chemoradiation
extra: Same reflex for airway obstruction, SVC syndrome, and painful bone mets: ask what the goal is first.

front: What is the standard treatment for limited-stage small cell lung cancer?
back: Cisplatin/etoposide with concurrent thoracic RT started early (45 Gy in 30 twice-daily fractions, or 60-66 Gy daily), then durvalumab
extra: Turrisi established 45 Gy BID; CONVERT found 66 Gy daily about equal. ADRIATIC added durvalumab.

front: Why is prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) considered in small cell lung cancer?
back: Small cell has a high risk of brain metastases, so responders get PCI (25 Gy in 10 fractions) or close brain MRI surveillance.
extra: MRI surveillance is increasingly used instead of PCI, especially in extensive stage.

front: What is the backbone treatment for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, and when is thoracic RT added?
back: Platinum/etoposide plus immunotherapy (atezolizumab or durvalumab). Consolidative thoracic RT is added for good responders.
extra: IMpower133 and CASPIAN set the chemo-immunotherapy standard. Palliative RT for symptoms.
